newsitem.title: USA: Pork belly prices soar on talk of Japanese demand.
newsitem.headline: Pork belly prices soar on talk of Japanese demand.

text.p: Pork belly prices soared on Thursday on buying sparked by talk that Japan was in the market looking to buy supplies from the United States.
"The usage between now and mid-August (in Japan) is pretty strong, so a lot of people think they are buying some extra to fill in for needs," said Chuck Levitt, an analyst with Alaron Trading Corp.

He noted that Japan's Obon holiday, which extends through mid-August, was normally a period of high meat consumption. Although any shipments would not arrive in time for the holiday, they would replenish Japanese stocks, which already stand about 25 to 30 percent below a year ago.

At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, pork belly futures for July delivery closed the three-cent daily limit higher at 85.80 cents a lb. The market had been tumbling, with July closing the three-cent limit lower on Wednesday.
Oil prices closed higher on the New York Mercantile Exchange, with gasoline continuing to lead the way.
Traders had differing views about whether the rally in gasoline was likely to be sustained, but most agreed that the looming renewal of Iraqi crude oil exports was likely to weigh on crude.

"A lot of people are confused. Everyone knows Iraqi oil is coming back but the market continues to hold and that is a positive sign," said Thomas Blakeslee, a trader at Cargill Investors Services in New York.
The front-month gasoline contract has moved up sharply in the past month, gaining eight cents or so from a low in late June of 54.85 cents.

The move has been supported by recent statistics showing an apparent surge in gasoline demand and anticipated tighter gasoline supplies on the East Coast because of maintenance at Tosco Corp.'s Bayway, New Jersey, plant, the region's biggest supplier of gasoline.

"Even though we've seen a little profit-taking in the afternoon, gasoline in the (New York) harbor is still quite steady and I don't know if it is quite over yet," said Gerry Samuels, a trader and analyst at ARB Oil in New York.

NYMEX gasoline for delivery in August, which expires next Thursday, rose 1.09 cents to settle at 62.21 cents a gallon. September crude was up 14 cents at $19.77 a barrel, while August heating oil gained 0.11 to 53.39 cents.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybean futures for August delivery rose sharply, boosted by talk that supplies from the United States were being used to fill export orders that had originally been slated to come from Brazil.
"They're talking about shifting beans from Brazil to U.S. origin," said Vic Lespinasse, a trader with Dean Witter.

Indications are that a cargo of soybeans (about 50,000 tonnes) sold by Brazil for August shipment was switched to U.S. origin, trade and U.S. export sources said. There was talk the soybeans were sent to Europe out of the Great Lakes.
CBOT August soybeans closed 13 cents a bushel higher at $7.52 a bushel.
Prices for soybeans to be delivered after this year's U.S. harvest, which normally takes place around October, were lower, however, as the crop continued to flourish.

The National Weather Service six- to 10-day weather outlook called for normal to below normal temperatures with normal to above normal rainfall. That scenario allayed fears that persistent hot, dry weather would damage crops.
Soybeans for November delivery finished down 1-1/4 cents at $6.01-3/4 a bushel.
